explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF enables row-count messages for the procedure's many statements.
XACT_ABORT is explicitly disabled despite later explicit transactions, allowing some runtime errors to leave transactions active.
@CustomerIdText embeds customer identifier N'1' instead of using the supplied customer parameter.
@OrderID is initialized with business identifier 1 rather than an input or lookup.
SELECT * retrieves every Orders column, including several nvarchar(max) columns, and couples the result schema to table changes.
TOP (10) selects an unspecified subset of Orders because no ORDER BY is present.
Orders.OrderID is the primary key, so DISTINCT cannot remove any duplicates.
NOLOCK permits dirty reads and can return missing or duplicated Orders rows.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) filters a computed date part instead of expressing a directly searchable OrderDate range.
The order-year filter embeds 2016 rather than accepting a reporting period.
CustomerID is int but @CustomerIdText is nvarchar(20), requiring implicit conversion of the variable to int.
The optional CustomerID OR predicate combines unfiltered and selective access paths in one statement, complicating plan selection.
LIKE N'%urgent%' requires substring matching rather than a normal prefix index seek.
The business search term 'urgent' is embedded in the Comments predicate.
ISNULL is applied directly to indexed CustomerID in the predicate; CustomerID is NOT NULL, so the wrapper is unnecessary.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) obscures a direct CustomerID comparison and relies on optimizer simplification to remove the unnecessary wrapper.
ISNULL embeds 0 as an undocumented fallback customer identifier.
The predicate embeds customer identifier 1 instead of using @CustomerID.
Adding zero to OrderID is unnecessary arithmetic on the indexed predicate column.
CustomerID <> 1 excludes a single customer and can require reading a broad portion of Orders.
The excluded customer identifier 1 is hard-coded.
TOP (1) returns an arbitrary Orders/Customers pair without ORDER BY.
CROSS JOIN combines Orders with unrelated Customers rows without a relationship predicate.
TOP (1) chooses an unspecified matching Orders/OrderLines row.
Orders and OrderLines use a comma-separated FROM list with their relationship placed in WHERE.
The scalar OrderLines count is correlated to each outer OrderID and can introduce repeated aggregate lookups.
The OrderLines existence subquery references each outer OrderID; a join to distinct qualifying OrderID values can express the same set without multiplying rows.
Quantity > 1 embeds an unexplained order-line quantity threshold.
The Comments-nullability CASE expression is repeated in ORDER BY instead of referencing HasComments.
ORDER BY 2 depends on the position of OrderDate in the SELECT list.
OrderDate is not unique, so OFFSET/FETCH can select inconsistent page boundaries without an OrderID tie-breaker.
The primary-key predicates OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2 produce unique, disjoint results, making UNION duplicate elimination unnecessary.
The first UNION branch embeds order identifier 1.
The second UNION branch embeds order identifier 2.
COUNT(*) > 0 computes an OrderLines count when only the existence of a matching line is needed.
The scalar COUNT subquery is correlated to each outer Orders row and can introduce repeated aggregate work.
Multiple Orders rows can assign @OrderID; the retained value is unspecified because the query has no ordering or single-row restriction.
TOP (5) inserts an arbitrary subset of OrderID values into @OrderIds.
SELECT INTO derives #ImplicitOrders' schema implicitly from the query rather than declaring it explicitly.
TOP (5) populates #ImplicitOrders with an unspecified subset of Orders.
order_cursor uses cursor allocation, opening, and fetching to retrieve an OrderID that a direct query could retrieve.
The cursor's TOP (2) query has no ORDER BY, so its candidate OrderID values are unspecified.
@CustomerID is converted to text and concatenated into SQL, producing value-specific statement text instead of a parameterized query.
EXEC (@Sql) executes SQL containing an embedded CustomerID without parameter binding.
@OrderID is concatenated into executable SQL instead of being represented by a bound parameter.
sys.sp_executesql receives no parameter definitions or values even though the statement filters by @OrderID.
#Scratch is explicitly created but never explicitly dropped before the procedure ends.
The CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE(), allowing execution to continue without propagating failure.
The negative-order-ID error path uses legacy RAISERROR instead of THROW.
PRINT emits a buffered diagnostic message rather than a structured result or error.
The Orders filter embeds customer identifier 1 instead of using @CustomerID.
The OrderDate cutoff '20160101' is an unlabelled, hard-coded reporting boundary.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits a style, so session date settings can change whether the result is January 2 or February 1.
The date constant '01/02/2016' is embedded directly without a named parameter or explanation of its purpose.
TOP (1) returns an unspecified matching Orders/Invoices row without ORDER BY.
COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) unnecessarily wraps the NOT NULL Orders join key.
COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) unnecessarily wraps the NOT NULL Invoices join key.
COALESCE is applied directly to indexed Orders.CustomerID in the join predicate instead of using the key directly.
COALESCE is applied directly to indexed Invoices.CustomerID in the join predicate instead of using the key directly.
The Orders-side COALESCE embeds undocumented customer fallback identifier 0.
The Invoices-side COALESCE embeds undocumented customer fallback identifier 0.
TOP (1) selects an arbitrary OrderID without ORDER BY.
Orders is joined to itself on its primary key, but o2 contributes no additional columns or filtering.
Sorting all Orders by Comments uses an nvarchar(max) sort key, increasing comparison cost and potential memory or tempdb usage.
SUM(Quantity) aggregates the entire fact-like OrderLines table without a restrictive predicate.
HAVING OrderID > 0 filters the grouping key rather than an aggregate and belongs in WHERE.
COUNT(*) counts the entire Orders table without a restrictive predicate.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns exactly one row, so ORDER BY OrderCount has no effect.
MERGE is used for a matched-only update, introducing unnecessary MERGE complexity and its associated correctness edge cases.
The MERGE action assigns target.Comments to itself, changing no value while potentially taking write locks and firing update triggers.
SET Comments = Comments changes no value while potentially taking write locks and firing update triggers.
DELETE selects OrderLines solely by Quantity rather than a key or order scope, potentially deleting unrelated lines.
Quantity = -1 embeds an unexplained deletion sentinel.
WAITFOR DELAY deliberately suspends procedure execution for one second and consumes server execution resources.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is outside TRY/CATCH, so transaction failures have no local cleanup handler.
IDENTITY_INSERT is enabled for Sales.Orders, but the supplied table definition has no identity column, so this statement fails when reached.
sp_who is invoked without its sys schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is not reset within the procedure, truncating subsequent result sets and limiting subsequent INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations to one row.
The VALUES insert into #DemoCategories relies on the table's physical column order.
The inserted CategoryID is hard-coded to 99.
The INSERT SELECT into #DemoCustomers omits target columns and relies on their declaration order.
The CustomerName pattern starts with '%', preventing a normal prefix seek on the unique CustomerName index.
@CustomerName is concatenated into executable SQL instead of supplied as a bound parameter.
Unescaped user-supplied @CustomerName is embedded inside a SQL string literal and executed on the next line, permitting SQL injection.
The generated CustomerName LIKE predicate begins with '%', requiring substring matching.
sp_executesql executes the concatenated CustomerName input without parameter definitions or bound values.
sp_executesql is called without its sys schema qualifier.
The #DemoCustomers update has no WHERE clause; the still-active ROWCOUNT 1 makes it update an arbitrary customer rather than an explicitly selected customer.
CustomerCategoryID is assigned hard-coded category identifier 1.
The WHERE predicate on o.OrderDate rejects NULL-extended rows, making the LEFT JOIN behave as an INNER JOIN and excluding customers without qualifying orders.
The OrderDate cutoff '2016-01-01' is embedded directly rather than supplied as a named reporting boundary.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL does not test for missing values; under ANSI NULL semantics it evaluates to UNKNOWN and returns no rows.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) is called in the SELECT list and can incur per-row function overhead unless eligible scalar UDF inlining applies.
The transaction's CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and does not rethrow or return a failure status.
The CATCH block does not roll back the transaction started in TRY, potentially leaving an active or uncommittable transaction.
WITH (INDEX = 1) forces the Customers access path by index ID and prevents the optimizer from freely selecting another index.
Three nested derived-table SELECTs pass through CustomerID without adding filtering or transformations, unnecessarily obscuring a simple query.
CustomerName LIKE '%A%' starts with a wildcard and prevents a normal prefix index seek.
The CustomerName substring criterion 'A' is hard-coded rather than supplied through a search parameter.
SELECT * exposes every column returned by dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti and makes callers dependent on its complete return schema.
